The study focuses on a generic engine containment segment for testing at Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 3.
The containment segment is approximately 51.4 arc angle (1/7 of the full structure) with an arc length of 420 mm and a height of 240 mm.
The composite material used is aerospace-grade prepreg CFRP with epoxy matrix and unidirectional carbon fibre reinforcement (CYCOM™ 977-2).
The manufacturing process involves high temperature autoclave curing up to 180°C and a pressure of 7 bar.
TEmSAL functional layers are based on Polyimide (PI) carrier foils with screen-printed conductive tracks and integrated piezo ceramic elements (PCEs).
The sensor network layout is tailored to the structure's first eight eigenmodes, with sensors placed in areas of high strain.
The functional layer is integrated between the second and third ply close to the back surface of the structure.
The layup sequence is [0/45/90/-45/0/45/90/-45/0/90] to minimize delamination tendency during impact loading.
Two containment segments, CO-1 and CO-2, were manufactured for testing.
External excitation tests used an instrumented impact hammer, and signals were recorded using a NI 5105 digitiser.
PCE2 and PCE3 were damaged during manufacturing, resulting in only noise being recorded from these sensors.
Self-sensing tests in pitch-catch configuration used PCE4 as the excitation source with a sinusoidal voltage signal of 2 kHz and 175 V amplitude.
PCE1, PCE5, and PCE6 recovered the input waveform with signal levels well above noise, while PCE2 produced only low-amplitude, disturbed signals.
The LFBO test used a compressed air gun with a barrel diameter of 80 mm and an impact velocity of 120 m/s.
The impactor was a laminated CFRP blade strip, 60 mm wide and 304 mm long, with a conical cross-section and 67 layers of CYCOM™ 977-2 at the root.
A custom sabot system with 3D printed endcaps and polymer spacer shells was developed to ensure stable positioning and clean separation of the impactor.
Post-impact ultrasonic transmission measurements revealed delamination in the areas of PCE2, PCE4, and PCE6, with a significant 44 mm by 34 mm delamination at the impact center around PCE4.
During the LFBO test, PCE4 failed due to severe damage, and PCE1 did not retrieve a usable signal due to failure of contacting.
The maximum signal value recorded by PCE5 during the LFBO test was 3.3 V, with an irreversible signal component of approximately 1.4 V.
The LFBO test setup is capable of reproducing the release blade behavior and main impact conditions on the containment, providing valuable validation data for numerical modeling.
Further improvements are needed to minimize sensor failure during integration and achieve consistent high quality in the TEmSAL manufacturing process.
A larger gas gun barrel would enable the inclusion of a full blade root with dove tail, allowing for more realistic impact scenarios.
The TEmSAL technology is suitable for implementing active condition and health monitoring systems for structures of comparable size.
The LFBO test configuration is a useful tool for de-risking containment tests and providing high-quality validation data for numerical modeling.
The study highlights the importance of real-time, autonomous monitoring of structural health for enhancing safety and reliability in aerospace structures.
